title: It is already on its way. Stop daring it to come.
subtitle: The Hour told in the past tense

row.title: the warning
sub: as if it were a bluff

then: Late in the Makkan years, the deniers kept daring the Prophet ﷺ to bring the punishment he warned of. They treated the delay as proof he was wrong. The verse speaks of the Hour {idea}in the past tense, as something already done{/idea}, and tells them {trap}not to rush it{/trap}.
now: The doctor said to cut back months ago. Nothing has happened, so the warning starts to feel like a joke. You scroll past reminders of death the same way. {idea}The quiet time is not a sign it is not coming. It is the time you were given to get ready.{/idea}
old: If it has not happened by now, it probably never will.
new: The delay is a gift of time, not a sign the promise is empty.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing until later in life. Do the first small step of it today.

title: Every message from above carried one line.
subtitle: What the angels brought to the prophets
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the Ruh here is {idea}revelation{/idea}, sent down by angels to the servants Allah chooses, the prophets. Their task was one: warn people that {idea}no one deserves worship but Allah{/idea}, and live mindful of Him.
now: You have saved a hundred reminders, lectures and posts. They blur together. Strip them down and almost all of them say the same thing: {idea}put Allah first, and nothing else in His place.{/idea} The rest is detail around that center.
old: Religion is a long list of things to keep track of.
new: Under every detail is one line: there is no god but Him.
try: Before you open your phone tomorrow morning, say la ilaha illa Allah once and mean it.

title: The sky and the earth were made for a reason.
subtitle: Creation with truth, not in vain
then: Ibn Kathir says the heavens and the earth were made {idea}for a true purpose, not in vain{/idea}, so that those who do wrong and those who do good each receive what they earned. Allah is above every partner people set up beside Him.
now: Late at night you wonder if any of it matters: the shift you pulled, the patience with your kid, the lie you did not tell. {trap}It can feel like nobody keeps count.{/trap} The verse says the whole sky above you was built {idea}on purpose{/idea}, and so was your small part in it.
old: The world just happens, and what I do disappears into it.
new: Everything was made with truth, so my choices are part of a real story.
try: Step outside tonight and look at the sky for one minute without your phone.

title: Made from a drop, then arguing with his Maker.
subtitle: How quickly the weak forget where they began

key.label: What we were made to be

then: Ibn Kathir notes that man begins as {idea}something weak and insignificant{/idea}. Once he can stand on his own, {trap}he starts to dispute with his Lord{/trap} and fight His messengers. But he was created to be a servant, not an opponent.
now: The first paycheck that covers rent. The promotion. The day you stop needing your parents' help. Somewhere in there a voice says {trap}I did this myself{/trap}. Look at a baby photo of yourself. {idea}You did not build the hands you work with.{/idea}
old: I am self-made and I answer to no one.
new: I started as almost nothing, and everything since then was given.
try: Look at an old photo of yourself as a baby and thank Allah for one thing you could not have done alone.

title: Your coat and your dinner both came from His care.
subtitle: Livestock as a gift you use every day

row.title: He created them for you
sub: a gift behind the price tag

then: For desert Arabs, livestock were life. Ibn Kathir lists the gifts: {reward}wool and hair for clothes and furnishings{/reward}, milk to drink, meat to eat. Ibn Abbas said the warmth here means clothing. The verse reminds them {idea}who made these animals for them{/idea}.
now: Your wool jumper, the milk in your tea, the leather of your shoes, the chicken in the fridge. {trap}You paid for them, so they feel like yours by right.{/trap} The verse traces them back one step further: {idea}He created them for you.{/idea}
old: I paid for it, so there is nothing to be thankful for.
new: Behind everything I paid for is something He made for me first.
try: At your next meal, name where one item on the plate came from and say alhamdulillah for it.

title: Even the beauty of a herd coming home is a gift.
subtitle: Allah counts beauty among His favors

row.title: beauty too
sub: joy for the eyes is a gift

then: After the practical uses, the verse adds {reward}beauty{/reward}. Ibn Kathir describes the herd brought home in the evening, their flanks full, udders heavy with milk, humps grown. And again when they go out in the morning. {idea}Allah names the pleasure of seeing them as a favor.{/idea}
now: Your kids spilling out of the car after school. A tidy shelf of plants you have kept alive. The street at sunset on your walk home. {idea}That small lift in your chest is also something given.{/idea} It does not have to be useful to be worth thanks.
old: Pretty things are extras, not real blessings.
new: Allah lists beauty among His gifts, so the joy of seeing is worth thanks too.
try: Notice one beautiful ordinary thing on your way home today and pause on it for five seconds.

title: They carry what would break your back.
subtitle: Kindness hidden in what bears your load

row.title: it was made subject to me
sub: by a Lord who is kind

then: Ibn Kathir lists the journeys: {reward}trade, Hajj, Umrah{/reward}, long trips to lands people could not reach without great hardship. The animals carried the loads. The verse ends by naming why: {idea}your Lord is Kind and Merciful{/idea}.
now: The bus that gets you to work. The car that carries the weekly shop. The delivery van, the plane that took you home for the funeral. {trap}You only notice them when they break down.{/trap} {idea}Each one is carrying weight you could never carry alone.{/idea}
old: Getting from place to place is just logistics.
new: Whatever carries my load was made easy for me by a kind Lord.
try: The next time you get in a car or on a bus, say subhan alladhi sakhkhara lana hadha.

title: And He creates what you do not yet know.
subtitle: Horses, mules, donkeys, and more to come
then: Ibn Kathir explains that horses, mules and donkeys were made mainly {reward}for riding and as adornment{/reward}, another blessing for travelers. Then the verse opens a door: {idea}He creates things you have no knowledge of{/idea}.
now: Your grandparents could not picture the phone in your pocket or the train you take to work. {idea}You do not know what will carry your grandchildren.{/idea} Every new thing you rely on was already in His plan before anyone invented it.
old: I already know the things that help me get through life.
new: There is always more He is creating than I have seen.
try: Think of one invention that made your life easier this week and thank Allah, not just the inventor.

title: Animals carry you over land. Allah shows the road to Him.
subtitle: From physical journeys to the journey of the soul
then: Ibn Kathir notes the Quran often moves from physical things to spiritual ones. After the animals that carry people on hard journeys, it speaks of {idea}the road that leads to Allah{/idea}. Ibn Abbas said it is up to Allah to make guidance and misguidance clear. Some roads {trap}swerve away{/trap}.
now: You plan a road trip carefully: map, fuel, rest stops. Then for the biggest questions of life you {trap}follow whatever your feed suggests{/trap}. The verse asks you to plan the inner journey at least as carefully, and to {idea}ask the One who made the road{/idea}.
old: Every path leads somewhere good if I mean well.
new: Some paths swerve, and Allah is the one who makes the straight one clear.
try: In your next prayer, say ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim slowly and actually ask for it.

title: Water falls from the sky, sweet enough to drink.
subtitle: Rain as drink for you and pasture for your herd
then: After the gift of livestock comes the gift of rain. Ibn Kathir points out that Allah {reward}made it fresh and pure to drink, not salty{/reward}, and from it grow the plants the cattle graze on. In dry Arabia, every listener knew what rain meant.
now: You turn the tap and fill a glass without thinking. {trap}It feels like it comes from the pipes.{/trap} Every drop started as rain that {idea}fell already drinkable{/idea}, on a schedule you did not set.
old: Water comes from the tap.
new: Every glass began as rain He sent down sweet enough to drink.
try: Drink your next glass of water sitting down, slowly, and say bismillah first.

title: One water, a thousand different fruits.
subtitle: A sign for people who think it through
then: Ibn Kathir highlights the wonder: {idea}with one kind of water{/idea}, the earth brings out plants of different tastes, colors, scents and shapes. Olives, dates, grapes, every fruit. This is a sign {reward}for people who give thought{/reward}.
now: You walk through the fruit aisle half-listening to a podcast. Bananas, oranges, dates, grapes. {idea}All of them drank the same kind of water.{/idea} The verse is not asking for more knowledge. It is asking you to stop and think for ten seconds.
old: Fruit is just food from the shop.
new: Different fruits from the same water point to the One who shapes them.
try: Pick up one fruit today, look at it for a moment, and think about where it came from before you eat it.

title: Night, day, sun, moon and stars all work on command.
subtitle: The sky runs on time for you
then: Ibn Kathir describes night and day following each other, the sun and moon moving in their orbits, the stars giving light to find the way. {idea}Each travels as it was ordained, without deviating.{/idea} These are signs {reward}for people who use their reason{/reward}.
now: Your alarm rings at six. The sun is right where it should be. You never worry it will forget to rise. {trap}That reliability is so total you never think about it.{/trap} {idea}Every sunrise is a command being obeyed.{/idea}
old: Sunrise is just how things work.
new: The sky keeps perfect time because it obeys, and it was set up to serve me.
try: Catch one sunrise or sunset this week and watch it to the end.

title: A world in every color, spread out for you.
subtitle: Variety on earth as a reminder

picture.label: What is spread on the earth

then: After the sky, the verse turns to the earth. Ibn Kathir lists its {reward}animals, minerals and plants{/reward}, all of different colors, shapes, benefits and qualities. It is a sign {idea}for those who remember Allah's blessings and thank Him{/idea}.
now: Your camera roll is full of food, faces, flowers, skies. You took them because something caught your eye. {idea}The variety itself is the message.{/idea} A grey world would have worked. He made it in color.
old: Colors and variety are just how nature looks.
new: The world did not need to be this varied. That it is, is a gift to remember.
try: Open your camera roll and find one photo of nature. Say alhamdulillah for the thing in it.

title: The sea feeds you, adorns you, and carries your trade.
subtitle: So that perhaps you will be grateful

row.title: use it and thank
sub: that is why it was given

then: Ibn Kathir describes the sea made subject to people: {reward}fish to eat, pearls and jewels to wear{/reward}, and ships plowing through it carrying goods from land to land. He notes the craft of shipbuilding goes back to Nuh. All of it so {idea}you may seek His bounty and be grateful{/idea}.
now: The tuna in your sandwich. The phone that was shipped across an ocean in a container. The pearl earrings your mother wore at her wedding. {trap}All of it arrived without you thinking of the sea once.{/trap} {idea}The verse ends with perhaps you will be grateful. That is the point.{/idea}
old: The sea is just a big, far-away thing.
new: Much of what I eat, wear and own crossed a sea He made calm for it.
try: Look at the label of one thing you own and see where it was shipped from. Thank Allah for the journey.

title: Mountains to steady the ground, rivers and roads to guide you.
subtitle: The earth arranged so you can find your way

picture.label: How the land is set up

row.title: it was made steady
sub: so you could live on it

then: Ibn Kathir explains that the mountains {idea}make the earth stable{/idea} so its creatures can live. Rivers rise in one place and {reward}bring provision to people in another{/reward}. Roads and gaps between mountains let people travel. All of it so that you may be guided.
now: You sleep in a house on ground that does not move. You drive a road someone cut through hills. The water in your city came from a river that started far away. {idea}Your whole life rests on things arranged before you arrived.{/idea}
old: Solid ground and open roads are just normal.
new: The steady ground under me and the roads in front of me were arranged for me.
try: On your next trip, notice one road, bridge or river along the way and say alhamdulillah for it.

title: Hills by day, stars by night, so no one stays lost.
subtitle: Landmarks placed for travelers who lose the way

picture.label: How a traveler finds the way

then: The surah is listing gifts one after another: the sea, the mountains, rivers and roads. Ibn Kathir explains the landmarks as {idea}great mountains and small hills that land and sea travelers use when they get lost{/idea}, and the stars as their guide in the darkness of night.
now: You drive home in the dark and know your exit by a lit tower. You find your friend's house by the blue gate. Your phone shows a dot on a map, guided by satellites in the sky. {idea}Someone placed markers before you ever needed them.{/idea}
old: Finding my way is just me being good with directions.
new: The markers I steer by were placed for me before I was born.
try: Next time you use a landmark or a map to find your way, say alhamdulillah for the sign.

title: The One who makes is not like what cannot make.
subtitle: A simple question after a long list of gifts
then: After naming the sea, the mountains, the rivers and the stars, the verse stops and asks the people of Makkah a plain question. Ibn Kathir says worship belongs to Allah alone, {trap}not to idols which do not create but are themselves created.{/trap} The verse ends: will you not reflect?
now: You catch yourself treating a boss, a follower count, or a lucky habit as if it decides your day. None of them made a single raindrop. {idea}Put them side by side with the One who made you, and the answer is obvious.{/idea}
old: Many things hold power over my life.
new: Only the One who creates has real power; the rest are created like me.
try: Write down one thing you fear or chase too much, then write next to it: created, like me.

title: You could never count His favors, and He still forgives.
subtitle: Gifts past counting, and mercy for falling short
then: This closes the long list of gifts. Ibn Kathir says if Allah asked people to thank Him for every blessing, {trap}they would not be able to do it.{/trap} So the verse ends with His names: {reward}He forgives much and rewards for little{/reward}, when people turn back to Him.
now: You try a gratitude list at night. Eyes, a bed, water from a tap, a mother who still calls. By item twenty you are tired and the list is barely started. {idea}The gap between what you got and what you thanked for is where His forgiveness sits.{/idea}
old: I am grateful enough; I say thanks now and then.
new: I can never thank Him enough, so I lean on His mercy for the gap.
try: Before sleep, name five favors from today out loud, then say: forgive me for the ones I missed.

title: He knows the hidden thought and the spoken word alike.
subtitle: No gap between private and public for Allah
then: The surah turns from gifts to the idols people called on. First it reminds them: Allah knows what is hidden in hearts as well as what is apparent. Ibn Kathir adds that {idea}everyone will be rewarded or punished for their deeds on the Day of Resurrection.{/idea}
now: You smile in the meeting while typing a different message under the table. You post a kind caption about someone you resent. {trap}The audience only sees one side.{/trap} {idea}He sees both, and He is the only audience that lasts.{/idea}
old: What I keep inside is my own business.
new: My hidden side is as open to Allah as my public face.
try: Pick one thing you say in public and check today whether your heart matches it.

title: What they call on made nothing; it was made.
subtitle: Idols cannot create, they are carved
then: Ibn Kathir links this to Ibrahim's words to his people: {trap}Do you worship what you yourselves carve,{/trap} {idea}while Allah created you and what you make?{/idea} The idols of Makkah were shaped by human hands, then asked for help.
now: You build a brand, a savings plan, a reputation, all with your own hands. Then slowly you start trusting it as if it holds you up. {trap}The thing you made becomes the thing you lean on.{/trap}
old: What I built will keep me safe.
new: What I built was made by me, and I was made by Allah.
try: Look at one thing you worked hard to build and thank Allah for the hands that built it.

title: Lifeless, unaware, not even knowing when the Hour comes.
subtitle: Why hope from what cannot hear or know
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the idols are inanimate, {trap}they do not hear, see, or think{/trap}, and do not know when the Hour will come. So how could anyone hope for benefit from them? {idea}Hope should go to the One who knows all things.{/idea}
now: You refresh the app hoping the numbers will tell you whether you are worth something. You check a horoscope before an interview. {trap}None of these know your tomorrow.{/trap} Only One knows when every story ends.
old: Something out there can tell me how things will turn out.
new: Only Allah knows what is coming, so my hope goes to Him.
try: Next time you feel anxious about an outcome, make one short dua instead of checking again.

title: One God, and the proud heart that refuses it.
subtitle: Denial starts in the heart, then shows as pride
then: After all the signs, the verse names the real problem. Ibn Kathir says the hearts of the disbelievers were {trap}astonished that all the gods were made into one God{/trap}, and they were too proud to worship Allah alone. Not believing in a return to Him made the pride easy.
now: Someone gives you good advice and it is clearly right. Still, something in your chest pushes back, because it came from them, or because it means admitting you were wrong. {trap}That push is not logic. It is pride.{/trap}
old: I reject things when the argument is weak.
new: Sometimes I reject the truth because my pride does not want to bow.
try: Think of one piece of advice you dismissed lately and ask honestly if pride was the reason.

title: He sees the hidden pride, and He does not love it.
subtitle: Arrogance is known even when it is quiet
then: This follows the verse about proud hearts. Ibn Kathir says Allah knows what they conceal and reveal and {trap}will requite them for it in full.{/trap} The verse ends with one line about the proud: He does not like them.
now: You never say it out loud, but you look down on the cleaner, the new hire, the cousin who did not go to university. {trap}Quiet pride is still pride.{/trap} {idea}Humility is something Allah loves, even in small hidden ways.{/idea}
old: As long as I do not show it, my pride does no harm.
new: Allah sees the pride I hide, and He does not love it.
try: Greet one person today you usually overlook, with full attention and a real smile.

title: Asked what was revealed, they said: just old stories.
subtitle: Dismissing a message without really answering

row.title: label it
sub: so I never have to listen

then: Ibn Kathir says when asked about the revelation, the leaders of Quraysh {trap}did not want to answer{/trap} and called it tales copied from earlier books. They had tried calling the Prophet ﷺ a sorcerer, a poet, a madman, then settled on what Al-Walid bin Al-Mughirah proposed: old magic passed down.
now: Someone shares a reminder in the family group chat and you think, oh, the usual stuff, and scroll. You never read it. {trap}A quick label saves you from having to listen.{/trap}
old: I already know what this is going to say.
new: Calling something old is not the same as answering it.
try: Read one reminder you would normally skip, all the way to the end.

title: Mislead others, and you carry part of their load too.
subtitle: Influence works in both directions
then: The leaders who called the Quran old tales did not only stray, they led others with them. Ibn Kathir quotes the hadith: {reward}whoever invites to guidance gets the reward of those who follow{/reward}, and {trap}whoever invites to misguidance bears the sin of those who follow{/trap}, without lessening anyone's share.
now: You forward a clip that mocks something sacred. Ten people share it on. You show a younger sibling a shortcut that cuts corners. {idea}Your influence keeps moving after you put the phone down.{/idea} It can carry good just as easily.
old: What others do with what I share is their choice.
new: What I pass on keeps counting for me or against me.
try: Share one beneficial thing today that you would be glad to have counted for you.

title: Their plans fell from the foundation up, from where unseen.
subtitle: Schemes against the truth collapse from below
then: Ibn Kathir notes some said this was Namrud and his tower, but the correct view is that it is {idea}an example for all who plotted against Allah's message.{/idea} He uprooted their efforts and brought them to nothing, {trap}from directions they did not perceive.{/trap}
now: You build something on a lie: a small fraud at work, a story you keep up. It holds for months. You watch the roof and feel fine. {trap}Collapse rarely comes from where you are watching.{/trap}
old: If nothing has gone wrong yet, my plan is safe.
new: A plan built against what is right can fall from its base without warning.
try: Check one thing you are building and ask: is the foundation honest?

title: Where are the partners you fought so hard for?
subtitle: The question asked on the Day of Resurrection
then: Ibn Kathir explains that on that Day, secrets are exposed and the Lord asks in rebuke: {trap}you fought and made enemies for their sake, so where are they now?{/trap} Those given knowledge then speak: disgrace and misery are on the disbelievers.
now: You fight your family over a career, lose friends defending a status, stay up nights for applause. {trap}Ask what you are making enemies for.{/trap} {idea}Will it stand next to you when it matters most?{/idea}
old: The things I fight for are worth the cost.
new: Some things I fight for will be nowhere when I need them.
try: Think of your last heated argument and ask what you were really defending.

title: At death they say: we did nothing wrong. He knows.
subtitle: The late denial at the last moment
then: Ibn Kathir describes those who wronged themselves when the angels come for their souls. {trap}They make it appear as if they had always listened and obeyed{/trap}, saying they did no evil. The reply is short: {idea}Allah knows what you did.{/idea}
now: You tell yourself you are basically a good person, so the small wrongs do not need fixing. The unpaid debt, the cold silence with your brother. {reward}The door to change is open now, while you still have time.{/reward}
old: I'm basically fine, nothing to answer for.
new: Allah already knows my record; honesty now is better than excuses later.
try: Fix one small wrong today: pay back, apologize, or return something.

title: Pride that would not bow ends in a wretched home.
subtitle: Where arrogance toward the signs leads
then: This continues the scene at death from the previous verse. Ibn Kathir explains it as {trap}a miserable place for those who were too arrogant to pay attention to the signs of Allah and follow His Messengers.{/trap} The verse names the arrogant directly.
now: Pride is quiet at first. You skip the prayer because you are busy, wave off the reminder, decide you know better. {idea}The verse shows where that habit points{/idea}, and {reward}every day you can still turn it the other way.{/reward}
old: A bit of pride is harmless; it is just confidence.
new: Pride that refuses Allah's signs is the thing that ruins a person's end.
try: Do one small act of worship today you have been putting off out of laziness or pride.

title: Asked what was revealed, the mindful said: something good.
subtitle: The same question, the opposite answer
then: Earlier the deniers called the revelation old fables. Now the same question goes to those who fear Allah. Ibn Kathir says they answer that {reward}He revealed something good: mercy and blessing for those who follow it.{/reward} The verse promises good in this world and better in the next.
now: Someone at work asks what Islam actually tells you to do. You could shrug, or you could say: it tells me to be honest, to look after my parents, to pray. {idea}How you describe what you received shows how you see it.{/idea}
old: Religion is a list of rules I have to put up with.
new: What Allah sent down is good, and doing good brings good here and better later.
try: Tell one person today one thing in the Quran you find genuinely good.

title: Gardens that last, rivers below, and whatever they wish.
subtitle: The home promised to the mindful
then: This describes the home called excellent in the verse before. Ibn Kathir says these are Gardens of Eternity where they live forever, {reward}rivers flowing between their trees and palaces{/reward}, with all that souls desire. He adds that this is how Allah rewards everyone who believes, fears Him, and does good.
now: Your flat is small, the rent is late, the commute is long. You scroll through pictures of homes you will never afford. {reward}There is a home with no rent, no lease ending, no moving out.{/reward} The way in is how you live now.
old: My best home is the one I can buy in this life.
new: The home worth working toward is the one that never ends.
try: Next time you feel envy over someone's house, ask Allah for a home in Paradise instead.

title: Taken in a good state, they hear: peace be on you.
subtitle: How the angels greet the righteous at death
then: This mirrors verse 28, where wrongdoers made excuses at death. Ibn Kathir says when death comes to believers {idea}free from shirk, impurity and evil{/idea}, the angels greet them and {reward}give them the good news of Paradise.{/reward} He links it to the angels who say: fear not, nor grieve.
now: You sit in a hospital corridor waiting for news about your grandmother. You think about how she prayed every day for sixty years. {reward}Death can arrive as a greeting of peace.{/reward} What you do today decides which welcome you get.
old: Death is only something to fear.
new: For the one who lived well, death opens with a greeting of peace.
try: Make a short dua today asking Allah for a good ending.

title: What are they waiting for, the angels at death?
subtitle: Delaying faith until it is too late
then: The verse asks the idolators of Makkah what they are waiting for. Ibn Kathir says {trap}only the angels coming to take their souls, or the Day of Resurrection.{/trap} Allah did not wrong them, because {idea}He sent Messengers and Books and made His proofs clear.{/idea}
now: You tell yourself you will start praying properly after the exams, after the wedding, after this busy season at work. {trap}The waiting has no end date you control.{/trap} The warning has already come.
old: I will get serious about faith later, when life calms down.
new: Waiting for later is a choice, and the warning has already reached me.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing for later and do the first small step today.

title: What they mocked is what surrounded them in the end.
subtitle: Deeds return to the one who did them
then: Ibn Kathir says these people {trap}used to make fun of the Messengers when they warned them{/trap} of Allah's punishment. In the end they were overwhelmed by the very thing they laughed at. It is the result of their own deeds, not an injustice.
now: Someone jokes about a warning sign: the health check, the debt, the ignored prayer. The group laughs and moves on. {trap}A joke does not change what is coming.{/trap} {idea}Taking it seriously early is mercy for yourself.{/idea}
old: If I can laugh about it, it can't be that serious.
new: Laughing at a warning does not make it untrue.
try: Stop yourself once today before joking about something sacred or serious.

title: If Allah wanted, we would not have done it, they said.
subtitle: Blaming fate for your own choices
then: The idolators of Makkah had made-up customs about certain animals with no revealed authority. Ibn Kathir says their argument was: {trap}if Allah hated what we did, He would have stopped us.{/trap} The reply: {idea}the Messengers clearly conveyed that it was forbidden.{/idea} Being allowed to do something is not approval.
now: You keep doing something you know is wrong and tell yourself: if Allah did not want this, He would not let it happen. The late nights on that app, the shortcut at work. {trap}Being able to do it is not permission.{/trap}
old: If it was really wrong, Allah would have stopped me.
new: Allah lets me choose, and His Messengers already told me what He wants.
try: Notice one time today you use fate as an excuse, and own the choice instead.

title: Every nation got a Messenger with one message.
subtitle: Worship Allah, avoid false gods, then see the results
then: Ibn Kathir says from Nuh, the first Messenger, until Muhammad ﷺ, {idea}all the Messengers brought the same message{/idea}: worship Allah alone and avoid false gods. Some were guided, some strayed. The verse tells listeners to {trap}travel and see what became of those who denied.{/trap}
now: You visit ruins on holiday: a fallen palace, an empty city that was once powerful. You take a photo and move on. {idea}The verse asks you to stop and think about why they fell.{/idea}
old: Old ruins are just history, nothing to do with me.
new: Every ruin is a reminder that the message reached them too.
try: Next time you see something old and fallen, pause and ask what lesson it holds for you.

title: Even your deepest wish cannot guide someone; Allah guides.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ who longed for them
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah told His Messenger ﷺ that {idea}his eagerness to guide them would not benefit them{/idea} if Allah willed otherwise. He cites Nuh telling his people that his advice would not profit them. It eases the weight on the one calling.
now: You worry about a sibling who has drifted away. You send articles, you argue, you lose sleep. {idea}Your care matters and your duas matter{/idea}, {reward}but the heart is in Allah's hand, not yours.{/reward}
old: If someone I love is not guided, I have failed.
new: I can call with love, but only Allah guides hearts.
try: Make a dua today for one person you have been trying to change, then let it rest with Allah.

title: They swore hard that the dead stay dead. Yes, they rise.
subtitle: A strong oath against a true promise
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolators {trap}swore fervently that Allah would not resurrect the dead{/trap}, thinking it impossible, and did not believe the Messengers. Allah's answer is one word, yes, and {idea}a promise He has bound Himself to.{/idea}
now: Your friend says, totally sure, that when you die that's it, lights out. They say it loudly, with confidence. {idea}Certainty in a voice is not proof.{/idea} The promise does not depend on who sounds surest.
old: If someone says it with total confidence, they probably know.
new: Loud certainty does not change Allah's promise that we will rise.
try: Spend two quiet minutes today thinking about standing before Allah one day.

title: The Day will settle every argument people had.
subtitle: Why the resurrection must happen
then: Ibn Kathir explains the wisdom of the resurrection: {idea}to make clear every dispute{/idea}, to reward those who did good and requite those who did evil, and so that {trap}those who swore it would never happen know they were lying.{/trap}
now: There is an argument in your family no one will ever win. The inheritance, who was right. You carry it for years. {reward}One Day all of it is made clear{/reward}, and you can stop needing to win it now.
old: If I don't prove I'm right now, the truth is lost forever.
new: Allah will make clear every argument; I don't have to win them all here.
try: Let go of one argument today you have been trying to win for too long.

title: He says Be, and it is. Raising the dead is easy.
subtitle: One word, no effort, no delay

row.title: one command
sub: like a blink of the eye

then: This answers the oath that the dead will not rise. Ibn Kathir says {idea}when Allah wants a thing, He only says Be, and it is.{/idea} He does not need to repeat or confirm it. He links it to the verse: Our command is but one, like the twinkling of an eye.
now: You feel your problem is too big for anyone to fix: the illness, the debt, the broken relationship. {reward}For the One who says Be, nothing is heavy.{/reward} That is a reason to ask Him with real hope.
old: Some things are too big even to pray about.
new: Nothing is hard for Allah; He only says Be, and it is.
try: Ask Allah today for the one thing you feel is too big to ask for.

title: They left home for Allah, and He gave them better.
subtitle: The emigrants who were wronged and then settled
then: Ibn Kathir says this may have been revealed about those persecuted so badly in Makkah that they {trap}left for Ethiopia to be able to worship their Lord{/trap}: Uthman bin Affan and Ruqayyah, Ja'far bin Abi Talib, Abu Salamah and others. {reward}Whoever gives up something for Allah, He compensates with something better.{/reward}
now: You turn down a job that would mean cutting corners. You move cities to protect your family's faith, leaving friends behind. It feels like pure loss. {reward}The verse says the account is not closed.{/reward}
old: What I give up for Allah is simply gone.
new: What I leave for Allah, He replaces with better, here and later.
try: Give up one small thing today purely for Allah's sake and trust Him with the gap.

title: Their two qualities: patience under harm, and trust in their Lord.
subtitle: What carried the emigrants through
then: This describes the emigrants of the verse before. Ibn Kathir says {idea}they bore their people's persecution with patience, putting their trust in Allah{/idea}, and {reward}He made their end good in this world and the Hereafter.{/reward}
now: The new country, the language you can't speak yet, the visa letter that has not come. You are tired of being strong. {idea}Patience is the holding on. Trust is knowing who holds you.{/idea}
old: I have to carry all of this by myself.
new: I hold on with patience and lean the weight on my Lord.
try: When the hard thing comes up today, say hasbiyallah and take one more patient step.

title: Every Messenger before was a man. Ask those who know.
subtitle: The objection that a Prophet cannot be human
then: Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas that some Arabs said {trap}Allah is too great to send a human being as a Messenger.{/trap} This verse answers them: ask the people of the earlier Books {idea}whether their Prophets were humans or angels.{/idea}
now: You are unsure about something in your faith and you are tempted to guess or let it go. The verse gives a simple method: {idea}ask the people who know.{/idea} A teacher, a scholar, a trusted imam.
old: If I don't understand it, I can just decide for myself.
new: When I don't know, I ask those who have knowledge.
try: Write down one question about your faith and ask a knowledgeable person this week.

title: The Quran came to the Prophet ﷺ so he could explain it.
subtitle: Signs, Books, and a teacher who makes it clear
then: The earlier Messengers came with clear signs and Books. Ibn Kathir says the Quran was sent to the Prophet ﷺ {idea}so he could explain in detail what was mentioned in brief, and make clear what was not clear.{/idea} Then the goal: that people {reward}examine themselves and be guided.{/reward}
now: You hear a verse in the taraweeh prayer and it sounds beautiful, then it is gone. You never look up what it meant or how the Prophet ﷺ lived it. {idea}The explanation is there. Reflection is the part left to you.{/idea}
old: Listening to the Quran is enough.
new: The Quran comes with an explanation, and it is meant to make me think.
try: Pick one short verse today, read how the Prophet ﷺ explained or lived it, and think on it.

title: Do the plotters of evil feel so safe?
subtitle: Patience from Allah is not permission
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells us about {idea}His patience, and how He delays punishment{/idea} for those who plot evil and call others to it, even though He is able to bring it on them {trap}in a way they do not know where it comes from.{/trap}
now: You keep a small scheme going: the fake receipts, the lie you tell your spouse. Months pass and nothing happens. {trap}Quiet is not the same as safe.{/trap} {reward}The delay is time given to stop.{/reward}
old: Nothing bad has happened, so it must be fine.
new: Allah's delay is patience giving me time, not a sign I'm safe.
try: Name one thing you are getting away with and end it today.

title: He could take them in the middle of their busy day.
subtitle: No one escapes by being occupied
then: Ibn Kathir explains going to and fro as {trap}when they are busy with their daily business, travel, and other distracting activities.{/trap} He links it to the verse asking if towns felt safe from punishment at night while asleep, or by day while playing.
now: Calendar full, inbox at 300, three trips this month. You never get a quiet minute to think about where life is going. {trap}Being busy feels like protection.{/trap} {idea}It is not; it only fills the time you could have used to turn back.{/idea}
old: I'm too busy right now to think about my akhirah.
new: My busy days can end at any moment, so I make room for Allah inside them.
try: Put a five-minute reminder in your calendar today just to sit and remember Allah.

title: Or seize them through what they fear, yet He is Kind.
subtitle: The threat ends with mercy
then: Ibn Kathir says this can mean taking from them {trap}what they most fear{/trap}, which is even worse. Then the verse ends: your Lord is Kind and Merciful, {reward}because He does not hasten to punish.{/reward} He quotes the hadith that no one is more patient with hurtful words than Allah, who still gives them provision and health.
now: You have said and done things you are ashamed of, and still you woke up today with breath, food, and family. {reward}That is His patience with you.{/reward} The right response is to use it, not test it.
old: Since I'm still fine, Allah must not mind what I'm doing.
new: I'm still fine because my Lord is patient and merciful, and that is a chance to return.
try: Thank Allah today for one blessing you still have despite a sin you regret.

title: Even shadows lean to the right and left in prostration.
subtitle: Every created thing bows in its own way
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}everything that has a shadow leaning right and left, morning and evening, is prostrating to Allah by its shadow.{/idea} Mujahid said the prostration of the mountains is their shadows. Abu Ghalib Ash-Shaybani said the waves of the sea are its prayers.
now: Late afternoon, you walk past a lamppost and its shadow stretches long across the pavement. Your own shadow beside it. {idea}Both bowing without a word.{/idea} The question is whether your heart is bowing too.
old: Shadows are just physics.
new: Even my shadow submits to Allah; my heart can too.
try: Notice your shadow once today and use it as a reminder to make one sajdah.

title: Everything in heaven and earth bows, and the angels without pride.
subtitle: Creatures and angels all prostrate
then: After the shadows, the verse widens to all creatures. Ibn Kathir says {idea}the angels prostrate to Allah and are not too proud to worship Him.{/idea} This answers those described earlier in the surah whose hearts were too proud.
now: Your cat stretches, the birds wake at dawn, a whole city hums. {idea}All of it in quiet obedience.{/idea} You are the one creature who can choose to join in, or hold back out of pride.
old: Bowing down feels like losing my dignity.
new: Everything bows to Allah; joining them is where dignity lies.
try: In your next prayer, stay in sujood a few breaths longer than usual.

title: They fear their Lord above them and do as commanded.
subtitle: Angels who obey without delay
then: Ibn Kathir says the angels {idea}prostrate out of fear of their Lord{/idea}, and they continually obey Allah, doing what He tells them and avoiding what He forbids. Their awe is not anxiety; it shows up as obedience.
now: You say you fear Allah, but the fear only appears as guilt at night. You worry, then do nothing. {idea}The angels' fear turns straight into action.{/idea} One obeyed command is worth more than hours of worry.
old: Feeling guilty is the same as fearing Allah.
new: Real fear of Allah shows in doing what He asks.
try: Turn one worry about your deen into one action today.

title: Do not take two gods. He is One, so fear Him.
subtitle: One God, one source of fear
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells us {idea}there is no god but He, and no one else should be worshipped except Him{/idea}, for He is the Sovereign, Creator, and Lord of all things. The command is short: do not take two gods, fear Me alone.
now: You fear your manager, your in-laws, what people will say at the wedding, and also say you fear Allah. {trap}A heart with many masters is always tired.{/trap} {idea}Fear the One, and the rest get smaller.{/idea}
old: I have to keep everyone happy.
new: When I fear only Allah, other fears lose their grip.
try: Next time you fear someone's opinion, ask: what does Allah think of this?

title: Everything is His, and worship is His forever.
subtitle: So who else is there to fear
then: Ibn Kathir reports that wasiba, the word for worship being His, means forever, or obligatory, or purely for Him. {idea}Worship is due to Him alone from all in the heavens and on earth.{/idea} Then the verse asks: will you fear anyone other than Allah?
now: You lie awake fearing a layoff, a diagnosis, a phone call. {idea}Every one of those is in His hands.{/idea} {reward}The One who owns all of it is the One who loves you best.{/reward}
old: There are many powers in my life I need to fear.
new: Everything belongs to Allah, so He is the only one worth fearing.
try: Name your biggest fear tonight and hand it to Allah in a short dua.

title: Every good you have is from Him, and you know it.
subtitle: In pain, everyone cries to the same door

row.title: you cry to Him
sub: no one else can fix it

then: Ibn Kathir says provision, blessings, good health and help all come from Allah's bounty. When harm comes, people cry to Him {idea}because they know none has the power to remove it except Him.{/idea} He cites the verse about danger at sea, when every false god vanishes except Him.
now: Turbulence on a flight, the plane drops, and the whole cabin goes quiet. Your lips are moving before you decide to pray. {idea}Your heart already knows whose door to knock on.{/idea}
old: I only really need Allah in emergencies.
new: The good days come from Him too, not only the rescue on bad days.
try: Make one dua today on a normal day, with nothing going wrong, just to thank Him.

title: Harm lifted, and at once some turn to other partners.
subtitle: The short memory after rescue
then: This continues the scene of crying to Allah in harm. Ibn Kathir says when He removes it, {trap}some associate others with their Lord{/trap}, the same pattern as the people at sea who turn away once safe on land.
now: You prayed every night while your father was in the ICU. He came home. Two weeks later you are telling everyone how good the hospital was, and the prayers have stopped. {idea}The rescue had a Rescuer.{/idea}
old: It worked out because the people and the plan were good.
new: When harm is lifted, I remember who I begged to lift it.
try: Think of one hard time Allah got you through and pray two rakahs of thanks for it.

title: Ungrateful for what He gave. Enjoy it, you will soon know.
subtitle: A short enjoyment and a coming realization
then: Ibn Kathir says they concealed the truth and denied the blessings Allah gave them, {idea}though He is the One who gives blessings and removes distress.{/idea} Then comes the warning: {trap}do what you like and enjoy it for a little while; you will soon know the consequences.{/trap}
now: Payday comes, the bonus lands, the holiday is booked. You enjoy it fully and never once think of who sent it. {idea}The enjoyment is short.{/idea} {reward}Thanks turns it into something that lasts.{/reward}
old: I earned this, so I can enjoy it however I want.
new: What I enjoy is a gift for a little while; gratitude is what lasts.
try: Before spending anything nice today, say alhamdulillah for it first.

title: They gave idols a share of what Allah provided them.
subtitle: Offering His gifts to what knows nothing
then: Ibn Kathir says the idolators {trap}gave their idols a share of what Allah had provided them{/trap}, and even gave preference to their gods over Him. So {idea}Allah swore by Himself to question them about these fabrications.{/idea}
now: Your time, money and energy come from Allah. Then most of it goes to things that cannot help you: the fan account, the endless shopping cart, the habit that drains you. {idea}A share always goes somewhere.{/idea}
old: How I split my time and money is my own business.
new: My provision is from Allah, and I will be asked where I sent it.
try: Look at where your money went this week and move one small amount toward something Allah loves.

title: They gave Him daughters and kept for themselves what they wanted.
subtitle: An unfair split, and a false claim about Allah
then: Ibn Kathir says they {trap}regarded the angels as females and called them Allah's daughters{/trap}, then worshipped them. They attributed offspring to Him, then chose for Him what they did not even want for themselves. The verse answers: {idea}Glorified is He.{/idea}
now: You keep the best for yourself and pass on what you don't want: the worse chair, the late shift, the leftover time for prayer. {trap}What we give Allah shows what we think of Him.{/trap}
old: Giving Allah what's left over is still giving.
new: What I hand to Allah shows how much I honor Him.
try: Give Allah the best part of your day once today: pray on time, before the other tasks.

title: Told of a baby girl, his face darkened with grief.
subtitle: Disappointment at a daughter's birth
then: Ibn Kathir describes the man in the days of ignorance who hears of a daughter's birth: {trap}his face becomes dark with distress, and he is silent from the intensity of his grief.{/trap} The same people called the angels Allah's daughters while hating daughters for themselves.
now: The scan shows a girl, and someone in the family sighs, maybe next time a boy. A small joke at the baby shower. {trap}The old disappointment still slips into words.{/trap} {reward}Every child is a gift from Allah.{/reward}
old: Hoping for a son over a daughter is just a preference.
new: A daughter is a gift from Allah, and grief at her birth is what the Quran condemns.
try: Say something warm and specific today about a girl or woman in your family.

title: Keep her in disgrace or bury her? Evil is their decision.
subtitle: The cruelty the Quran came to end
then: Ibn Kathir says the man {trap}hides from people so no one sees him{/trap}, and weighs keeping her in humiliation, without care or inheritance and behind his sons, or burying her alive, as was done in the days of ignorance. The Quran names it: evil is what they decide.
now: Today it looks quieter: the son gets the university fund, the daughter gets told to wait. The boy is praised, the girl is corrected. {trap}Unequal care is a smaller form of the same wrong.{/trap} {idea}Fairness between children is part of honoring them.{/idea}
old: Treating my children a bit differently is normal.
new: Treating a daughter as less is a wrong the Quran calls evil.
try: Notice one way you treat children around you differently by gender and even it out today.

title: The evil description is theirs; the highest belongs to Allah.
subtitle: Imperfection is human, perfection is His
then: After the claims about daughters, the verse sums up. Ibn Kathir says {trap}only imperfection is to be attributed to those who do not believe in the Hereafter{/trap}, while {idea}Allah is absolutely perfect in all ways, and this perfection is His alone.{/idea}
now: When something in life confuses you, you might picture Allah like a moody boss or a careless parent. {idea}Every picture of Him smaller than perfect is our flaw, not His.{/idea}
old: Sometimes Allah seems unfair, like people are.
new: Allah has the highest description; when I see a flaw, it is in my view.
try: Learn one name of Allah today and its meaning, and use it in your dua.

title: If He punished at once, nothing would be left walking.
subtitle: His patience holds the world until its term
then: Ibn Kathir says if Allah punished people for what they did, there would be no living creature left on earth. {reward}He is forbearing and covers people's faults{/reward}, waiting until the appointed time. He reports Abu Hurayrah hearing a man say the wrongdoer harms only himself, and replying: {trap}even the buzzard dies in its nest because of the sins of the wrongdoer.{/trap}
now: You tell yourself your bad habit is your business and hurts no one. Then you notice the mood at home, the kids copying you, the trust that thinned. {trap}Wrong leaks out.{/trap} {reward}The world keeps going because He is patient.{/reward}
old: My wrongs only affect me.
new: My wrongs ripple outward, and the world stands only by Allah's patience.
try: Think of one habit of yours that affects others and cut it back today.

title: Doing wrong while claiming the best will be theirs.
subtitle: Bad deeds with confident false hopes
then: Ibn Kathir says they {trap}combined bad deeds with false hopes of being rewarded with good{/trap}, which is impossible. He compares it to the man in his garden who said he did not think the Hour would come, and if it did, he would find better there.
now: You skip prayers, cut corners, and still say, Allah is merciful, I'll be fine. {idea}Mercy is real, and hope is good.{/idea} {trap}But hope with no effort is just a story you tell yourself.{/trap}
old: Allah is merciful, so it will all work out for me anyway.
new: Real hope in Allah's mercy comes with real effort to please Him.
try: Pair one hope you have from Allah with one action that matches it today.

title: Shaytan made their deeds look good. He is a useless ally.
subtitle: Comfort for the Prophet ﷺ and a warning

row.title: it was made to look nice

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah comforted His Messenger ﷺ: {idea}you have an example in your brothers among the Messengers{/idea}, who were also rejected. The reason was that {trap}Shaytan made their deeds attractive to them{/trap}, and on that Day he will be their only helper and cannot save them.
now: The ad makes debt look like freedom. The show makes cheating look romantic. Your own mind dresses up a grudge as justice. {trap}Wrong rarely looks ugly from the inside.{/trap}
old: If something feels good and looks good, it's probably fine.
new: Shaytan's work is to make wrong look attractive, so I check what is under the shine.
try: Pick one thing that looks appealing today and ask honestly: would Allah be pleased with it?

title: The Book came to settle disputes and to guide with mercy.
subtitle: Why the Quran was revealed

row.title: mercy
sub: for those who hold to it

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah revealed the Book to His Messenger ﷺ {idea}to explain the truth in matters people dispute over{/idea}, so the Quran is a decisive arbitrator for every argument. It is guidance for hearts and {reward}mercy for the one who holds to it.{/reward}
now: Your family is split over how to handle a hard situation. Everyone has opinions, a cousin forwards a video. {idea}The Book was sent to be the place you go first, not last.{/idea}
old: The Quran is for special occasions and prayer.
new: The Quran is meant to settle my real disputes and guide my real decisions.
try: Next time you disagree with someone about right and wrong, look up what the Quran says first.

title: Dead ground turns green. So can a dead heart.
subtitle: Rain as a picture of revelation
then: Just before this, Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ that the Book was sent to settle what people argue over, as guidance and mercy. Ibn Kathir links the two: {idea}as the Quran brings dead hearts to life, rain brings dead earth to life.{/idea} The sign is for those who truly listen.
now: You feel flat. Prayers on autopilot, nothing lands. Then one evening a single verse you have heard a hundred times stops you in the kitchen. {reward}That is rain on cracked ground.{/reward} The earth does not water itself, and neither does a heart.
old: My heart has been dry so long it will stay that way.
new: Allah revives dead ground every season. A dry heart is not a finished heart.
try: Listen to one short passage of Quran today with the meaning in front of you, and nothing else open.

title: Pure milk, made between waste and blood.
subtitle: The quiet miracle in an ordinary glass

row.title: a lesson
sub: wisdom, power, mercy of the Maker

then: The people of Makkah lived with camels, cows and sheep every day. Ibn Kathir explains that inside the animal, blood goes to the veins and milk to the udder, and {idea}none of them mixes with the other.{/idea} Something clean and sweet comes out of a place full of what is not clean.
now: You pour milk into your tea without looking, scrolling with the other hand. Somewhere a cow turned grass into this, and kept it apart from everything else in its body. {reward}Someone arranged that for you.{/reward} The ordinary is where the lesson hides.
old: Milk is a grocery item, nothing to think about.
new: Every ordinary glass is a lesson set in front of me by Allah.
try: Next time you drink milk or eat something simple, pause for three seconds and say alhamdulillah on purpose.

title: Same fruit, two roads: what clouds you, what feeds you.
subtitle: Reason as the gift worth protecting

row.title: people who reason
sub: the noblest thing in a person

then: The verse lists blessings from the date palm and the vine. Ibn Kathir notes it came before strong drink was forbidden, and that the verse already sets {trap}what intoxicates{/trap} apart from {reward}goodly provision.{/reward} It closes with reason, which he calls the noblest feature of a human.
now: The same phone can teach you something or eat four hours of your night. The same money can feed a family or chase a high. Most gifts come with two roads built in. {idea}A clear mind is how you tell which road you are on.{/idea}
old: A gift is a gift, whatever I do with it.
new: Allah gives the fruit and the mind. The mind decides which road the fruit takes.
try: Notice one thing today that fogs your thinking, and choose the clearer option once.

title: Even a bee is guided. It knows where to build.
subtitle: The surah's name, and a small creature's instruction

picture.label: Where the bee is told to live

then: The surah takes its name, An-Nahl, the Bee, from this verse. Ibn Kathir says the inspiration here means {idea}guidance.{/idea} The bee is shown where to settle, and it builds combs of interlocking hexagons with no looseness in them.
now: You are lying awake wondering if Allah has a plan for your job, your move, your marriage. Outside, a bee that has never been taught anything is building a perfect six-sided room. {reward}The One guiding her has not forgotten you.{/reward}
old: Nobody is guiding my life. I am figuring it out alone.
new: If Allah guides a bee to its home, He has not left me without direction.
try: Before one decision today, ask Allah for guidance in a single plain sentence.

title: Easy paths, then honey, then healing.
subtitle: What comes from following the way laid down
then: Ibn Kathir describes the bee flying far across the wilderness, then returning straight to its hive. Honey comes out {reward}white, yellow, red,{/reward} depending on what it ate, and in it is healing. He reports that a man's sick brother was told by the Prophet ﷺ to drink honey, again and again, until he recovered.
now: A tired evening, a sore throat, a spoon of honey in warm water. A creature smaller than your fingernail flew thousands of trips to make that spoon. {idea}It did not wander. It followed the path it was given,{/idea} and something healing came out.
old: Honey is just something sweet in the cupboard.
new: A weak creature following its Lord's path produces healing. That is the sign.
try: Have a spoon of honey today and think, for one moment, about the bee that made it.

title: You learned everything. One day you may know nothing.
subtitle: Strength is on loan, and so is memory
then: Allah created people and will take them back. Some He lets grow very old, until they {trap}know nothing after having known.{/trap} Ibn Kathir reports that the Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge in Allah from laziness, old age and senility.
now: Your grandmother asks your name for the third time this visit. She once ran a whole household from memory. {idea}Her knowledge was a gift with an end date.{/idea} So is yours. The years you can still think clearly are the years to use.
old: I have plenty of time to learn and do good later.
new: My clear mind is on loan. Its best years are the ones I have now.
try: Call or visit an elderly relative today and be patient with them, as you would want someone to be with you.

title: You would not share your wealth as equals. Yet you share Allah's?
subtitle: An argument from your own pocket

row.title: He has no partner
sub: they would not accept it themselves

then: The idolaters' pilgrimage chant admitted their partners were owned by Allah, yet still called them partners. The verse uses their own life: {trap}you would never let your servant share your wealth equally,{/trap} so why give Allah's servants a share in His divinity? Ibn Kathir also cites Umar writing that differences in provision are {idea}a test for both sides.{/idea}
now: Your colleague earns more. Your cousin earns less. You might feel proud, or bitter, or both in the same week. The verse says the gap is not a ranking of worth. {idea}It is a test, handed out by the One who owns all of it.{/idea}
old: What I have is mine, and what they lack is their problem.
new: Allah set the differences in provision. Each of us is tested by our share.
try: Thank Allah for one thing you have that someone close to you does not, then quietly help them with it.

title: Spouse, children, grandchildren, food. Then who gets the credit?
subtitle: The family around your table is a favor
then: Ibn Kathir explains that mates were made of our own kind so there could be {reward}harmony, love and mercy.{/reward} Children and grandchildren follow. The verse then asks how people could thank false gods for all this. He cites a hadith that on the Day, Allah will remind a servant: did I not give you a spouse?
now: Eid lunch. Your spouse laughing in the kitchen, the kids fighting over the last samosa, your mother holding the baby. You think, I worked hard for this. {idea}You did. And every face at that table was given.{/idea}
old: My family is the result of my choices and my effort.
new: My spouse, my children, the food on the table are favors from Allah first.
try: Tell one family member today, out loud, that you are grateful to Allah for them.

title: They cannot make a single drop of rain.
subtitle: Worshipping what provides nothing
then: The people of Makkah depended on rain and crops, yet worshipped idols. Ibn Kathir says these could not make {trap}rain fall or plants grow,{/trap} not even for themselves if they wanted to. Only Allah is the Provider.
now: The job offer, the boss's mood, the client who keeps the business alive. You check your inbox like it holds your whole future. {idea}None of them can send rain.{/idea} They are channels, not sources.
old: My income depends on this boss, this client, this market.
new: People and markets are channels. The provision itself comes only from Allah.
try: Before checking work messages tomorrow morning, say one short dua asking Allah for provision.

title: Do not draw Allah in the shape of anything.
subtitle: He knows, and we do not

row.title: I can picture Him
sub: like a king, like a person

then: Following the idols that provide nothing, the verse tells people {trap}not to set up examples or rivals for Allah,{/trap} nor describe anything as being like Him. Ibn Kathir says Allah knows and bears witness that there is no god but Him, {idea}while people associate others out of ignorance.{/idea}
now: In a hard week you catch yourself thinking Allah is like a tired manager who stopped reading your emails. Or like a strict parent who is never pleased. {idea}Those pictures come from your world, not from Him.{/idea}
old: I imagine Allah the way I imagine powerful people I know.
new: Allah is not like anything I can compare. I learn about Him from what He says.
try: Read the meaning of one of Allah's names today and replace one wrong picture with it.

title: One can do nothing. One gives freely, seen and unseen.
subtitle: A parable of two servants
then: Ibn Abbas said this compares the disbeliever and the believer. Mujahid said it compares an idol with the True God. Either way, {trap}one has power over nothing{/trap} and {reward}the other gives from good provision, in secret and in public.{/reward} The difference is so plain only a fool would miss it.
now: Two people in the same office earn the same salary. One spends it all on himself and feels stuck. The other quietly pays a colleague's bus fare and gives openly at the mosque drive. {reward}Same money, very different person.{/reward}
old: What I do with my money in private does not really matter.
new: Giving in secret and in public is what makes a provided person different.
try: Give something small today that nobody will ever know about.

title: A burden who brings no good, beside one who commands justice.
subtitle: The second parable: two men again
then: Mujahid said this again compares idols with the True God: {trap}the idol cannot speak, cannot act, and is carried by its owner.{/trap} Ibn Abbas said it is also the disbeliever and the believer. {idea}The other man commands fairness and walks straight.{/idea}
now: In the family group chat, one cousin only complains and never shows up when help is needed. Another quietly organizes, settles the argument fairly, and does what she said she would. {idea}You know which one you want to be.{/idea}
old: As long as I am not harming anyone, I am fine.
new: The verse praises the one who brings good and stands for fairness, not just avoids harm.
try: In one disagreement today, say the fair thing even if it does not favor you.

title: The Hour is a blink away, or nearer.
subtitle: The unseen belongs to Allah alone

row.title: a twinkling of the eye
sub: for the One who wills it

then: Makkah's leaders mocked the Prophet ﷺ, asking him to hurry the punishment. This verse answers: only Allah knows the unseen, and {trap}the Hour comes as fast as a blink of the eye, or faster.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains that when Allah wills a thing, {idea}He only says Be, and it is.{/idea}
now: You keep a list in your head: the apology you will make next year, the prayer habit you will start after exams, the debt you will settle later. {trap}Later is a guess.{/trap} The blink you are in right now is the one you actually have.
old: There will be time to fix things before the end.
new: The end is not far for Allah. The moment to fix things is this one.
try: Pick one thing on your someday list and do the first step of it today.

title: Born knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and a heart.
subtitle: The tools you use every day were gifts
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah brought people out of the womb knowing nothing, then gave them hearing, sight, and reason, which grow gradually until they peak. {idea}He created these faculties so a person can worship his Lord with them.{/idea} He quotes the hadith where Allah becomes the hearing and sight of the servant He loves.
now: You hold a newborn niece who cannot yet focus her eyes. Then you look at your own hands typing, your ears catching music, your mind making plans. {reward}All of it was handed to you.{/reward} {idea}Thanks means using it well.{/idea}
old: My mind and senses are simply mine.
new: Every sense I have was given to me so I could be grateful with it.
try: Choose one thing today you will not look at or listen to, as thanks for your eyes and ears.

title: Birds held in the open sky, and only Allah holds them.
subtitle: A sign you can see from any window
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells His servants to look at the birds between heaven and earth: {idea}they are held up only by Him, who gave them strength and subjected the air to carry them.{/idea} He links it to Surat Al-Mulk: none holds them up except the Most Gracious.
now: You are stuck in traffic and a flock of birds turns together over the bridge. {idea}Nothing holds them up but Him.{/idea} {reward}The same One holds up your day.{/reward}
old: Birds flying is just ordinary.
new: Every bird in the sky is held up by Allah, and so am I.
try: Watch a bird for thirty seconds today and say subhanallah.

title: Your home is rest, your tent is light, your rug is wool.
subtitle: Ordinary comforts listed as His blessings
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah gave people homes to live in and protect themselves, and tents of leather {reward}light and easy to carry on journeys{/reward}. From the wool of sheep, fur of camels and hair of goats come carpets, clothing and goods for trade, {idea}comfort until the appointed time.{/idea}
now: You get home after a long shift, kick off your shoes, sink into the sofa under a soft blanket. {reward}Rest has a Giver.{/reward} The home is for a while; gratitude for it can last.
old: My home and comforts are just things I bought.
new: My home and its comforts are blessings from Allah, given for a while.
try: When you walk into your home tonight, say a short thanks to Allah for a place to rest.

title: Shade, shelter, clothes for heat, armor for battle: favor completed.
subtitle: Protection given so you can submit to Him
then: Ibn Kathir explains the shade as trees, the refuges as fortresses, the garments as cotton, linen and wool, and the armor as iron mail. {idea}He gives what you need to go about your business, so it helps you worship and obey Him.{/idea}
now: A hot summer day, you find the one tree in the car park and stand in its shade. Your sunglasses, your coat, your locked front door. {reward}Each is a small protection.{/reward} {idea}Each frees you for something more.{/idea}
old: Protection and comfort are the point of life.
new: Allah protects me so I can live for Him.
try: Next time you find shade or shelter, use the moment to say alhamdulillah.

title: If they turn away, your job was only to make it clear.
subtitle: Relief for the one who delivers the message
then: After all the reminders of blessings, the verse turns to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Kathir says: {idea}after this declaration and reminder, do not worry about them{/idea}; your duty is to convey the message clearly, and you have done it.
now: You explain to your teenage son, gently and clearly, why something matters. He rolls his eyes and walks off. {idea}You said it well.{/idea} {reward}What happens in his heart is not your burden to carry alone.{/reward}
old: If they don't listen, I didn't say it right.
new: My part is to say it clearly and kindly; the rest is with Allah.
try: Say one piece of good advice clearly today, then let go of how it's received.

title: They know the favor is from Allah, then deny it.
subtitle: Knowing and acknowledging are not the same
then: Ibn Kathir says {idea}they know Allah is the One who grants these blessings{/idea}, but {trap}deny it by worshipping others and thinking their help and provision come from others besides Him.{/trap}
now: Asked about your success, you list your degree, your hustle, your contacts. You know deep down Allah opened every door. {trap}You just don't say it.{/trap} Knowing without acknowledging is a quiet denial.
old: I know it's from Allah; I don't need to say it.
new: Knowing a gift is from Allah means crediting Him for it out loud.
try: When someone praises you today, add: it's from Allah.

title: A witness from every nation, and no room for excuses.
subtitle: When the time for apologies has passed
then: Ibn Kathir says on that Day Allah will raise a witness from every nation, {idea}their Prophet, to testify about their response to the message.{/idea} Those who disbelieved {trap}will not be allowed to offer any excuse, nor return to the world to repent.{/trap}
now: You keep a draft apology to your friend saved in your phone. You'll send it when the time is right. {reward}Excuses and apologies have a window, and it is now.{/reward}
old: I can always explain myself later.
new: The time to repent and explain is now, not on that Day.
try: Send the apology or make the tawbah you have been putting off, today.

title: Once they see it, there is no lightening and no delay.
subtitle: The respite of this life will end
then: Ibn Kathir says when the wrongdoers see the punishment, {trap}it will not be reduced for them even for a moment, nor delayed.{/trap} Earlier in the surah, Allah's patience delayed punishment. Here, that delay is over.
now: Today you still have the delay: another morning, another chance to pray, to return a debt, to make up with a parent. {reward}This is the respite.{/reward} {idea}The verse is a reason to use it, not fear it.{/idea}
old: There will always be more time to fix things.
new: The time I have now is the respite; one day it ends.
try: Do one thing today you would want done if this were your last week.

title: They point at their partners, and the partners call them liars.
subtitle: What you relied on turns against you
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}their gods will disown them when they need them most{/trap}, saying: you are lying, we never commanded you to worship us. He links it to Ibrahim's words: on the Day of Resurrection you will disown each other.
now: You followed the crowd at work into something shady because everyone was doing it. When it comes out, every one of them says, I had nothing to do with it. {trap}The people you go along with won't stand with you later.{/trap}
old: If everyone does it, we'll all stand together.
new: Those I follow instead of Allah will disown me when it matters.
try: Notice one thing you do only because others do, and ask whether Allah wants it.

title: Everyone surrenders that Day; the inventions just disappear.
subtitle: What was made up wanders away
then: Qatadah and Ikrimah said they will humble themselves and surrender on that Day. Ibn Kathir adds {idea}there will not be anyone who does not hear and obey{/idea}, and the things they worshipped, {trap}based on fabrications and lies, will all disappear.{/trap}
now: You build your sense of safety on stories: my job is secure, my looks will last, my followers love me. {trap}One day each story wanders off.{/trap} {reward}Bowing to Allah now, by choice, is the only surrender that is rewarded.{/reward}
old: I'll submit when I'm sure.
new: Everyone will submit that Day; submitting now is what counts.
try: Make one sajdah today with the intention: I choose You now.

title: Those who blocked others' way get a heavier load.
subtitle: Turning people away is its own wrong
then: Ibn Kathir says this means {trap}one punishment for their disbelief and another for turning others away from the truth.{/trap} He links it to those who forbade others from following the Prophet ﷺ while keeping away themselves.
now: Your friend says she wants to start wearing hijab or praying, and you laugh, or say, it's not for people like us. {trap}A small comment can block someone's way.{/trap} {idea}A small word of support can open it.{/idea}
old: Teasing someone about faith is harmless.
new: Turning someone away from good is a serious wrong; helping them toward it is a gift.
try: Encourage one person today who is trying to grow closer to Allah.

title: The Prophet ﷺ will witness over his people. The Book explains everything.
subtitle: A witness and a Book for this ummah
then: Ibn Kathir reports that when Ibn Mas'ud recited from An-Nisa to the Prophet ﷺ and reached the verse about him being a witness over these, he said: enough. Ibn Mas'ud said {idea}he turned and saw his eyes streaming with tears.{/idea} The Book was sent as an explanation of everything, {reward}guidance, mercy and good news.{/reward}
now: Picture the Prophet ﷺ, who wept thinking of being witness over his people, asked about you. Your prayers this week, your Quran that sits on the shelf. {idea}He cared enough to cry for you.{/idea}
old: The Prophet ﷺ is a figure from history, far from my life.
new: The Prophet ﷺ will witness over my response, and he wept for us.
try: Send salawat on the Prophet ﷺ ten times today, thinking of his care for you.

title: Justice, kindness, family: commanded. Indecency, evil, aggression: forbidden.
subtitle: The most comprehensive verse, according to Ibn Mas'ud
then: Ibn Mas'ud said this is {idea}the most comprehensive verse in the Quran.{/idea} Ibn Kathir reports that Uthman bin Maz'un was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when it was revealed, and said that was when {reward}faith was established in his heart.{/reward} He quotes the hadith that aggression and cutting family ties are sins whose punishment comes quickly.
now: Your cousin wronged you over money. Justice says you can ask for it back. Kindness says you could let some go. Family says don't cut him off. {idea}One verse covers the whole family group chat.{/idea}
old: Being fair is enough; kindness is extra.
new: Allah asks for justice, then kindness on top, and to keep family close.
try: Reach out today to one relative you have drifted from, with a short kind message.

title: Keep the promise you made with Allah as your witness.
subtitle: Covenants and oaths are not to be broken
then: Ibn Kathir says this is one of Allah's commands: {idea}fulfill covenants, keep promises, and fulfill oaths after confirming them.{/idea} He explains it concerns covenants and agreements between people. The verse ends with {trap}a warning to those who break them: Allah knows what you do.{/trap}
now: You told your colleague you would cover her shift. You said wallahi I'll pay you back by Friday. Then something better came up. {idea}When you put Allah's name on your word, He becomes the witness.{/idea}
old: Plans change; people will understand if I back out.
new: A promise made in Allah's name is a trust I keep before Him.
try: Think of one promise you have not kept yet and keep it today, or tell the person honestly.

title: Don't be like her, undoing strong thread she spun herself.
subtitle: Breaking your word when a better side appears
then: Some said this was a foolish woman in Makkah who kept undoing her own strong thread. Ibn Kathir says the clearer meaning is {trap}one who breaks a covenant after confirming it.{/trap} Mujahid said people made alliances, then {trap}dropped them for a more powerful, more numerous party.{/trap} Allah tests people by this.
now: You commit to a friend's small startup, then a bigger company calls. You agreed to one family's proposal, then a richer one appears. {trap}Unraveling your word for a better deal.{/trap} {idea}The pull toward the bigger side is the test.{/idea}
old: If a better option comes, it's smart to switch.
new: Breaking my word for a better offer undoes my own strong thread.
try: Recommit today to one agreement you have been tempted to drop for something shinier.

title: He could have made you one community. You will still be asked.
subtitle: Differences exist, and each answers for their deeds
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah could have made all people one nation in harmony, with no differences or hatred. Instead He guides and lets stray as He wills. Then on the Day of Resurrection {idea}He will ask them all about their deeds{/idea}, even something as small as {trap}the thin membrane of a date stone.{/trap}
now: You see people arguing about faith online and think, what's the point, it's all written anyway. {idea}The verse says: you will be asked about what you did.{/idea} Your part is your own conduct.
old: Since guidance is in Allah's hands, my effort doesn't matter.
new: Guidance is His, and I will still answer for every small deed I do.
try: Do one small good deed today and remind yourself it will be counted.

title: A broken oath can make a firm foot slip.
subtitle: Betrayal pushes others away from Allah

row.title: a block on the path
sub: others judge the faith by it

then: Ibn Kathir explains the slipping foot as {trap}one who was on the right path but deviated because of a broken oath.{/trap} He says if a disbeliever made a covenant and the believer betrayed him, the believer would have {trap}hindered him from entering Islam.{/trap}
now: Your neighbor knows you pray. Then you don't return the money you borrowed. Your client knows you're Muslim, and you miss the deadline you swore to meet. {idea}People read your faith through your honesty.{/idea}
old: My broken promises only affect my reputation.
new: When I betray someone, I might be pushing them away from Allah.
try: Settle one outstanding promise to someone today, especially someone who knows you're Muslim.

title: Don't sell Allah's covenant for a small price.
subtitle: The whole world is a small price
then: Ibn Kathir says do not neglect an oath sworn in Allah's name {trap}for the sake of this world and its attractions, for they are few.{/trap} Even if a person gained the whole world, {reward}what is with Allah is better for him.{/reward}
now: A contract clause you promised to honor could be quietly ignored for a bigger profit. A witness statement could bend for a favor. {trap}Whatever they pay, it is a small price.{/trap}
old: Bending my word for a big enough gain is just business.
new: No price is big enough to trade my word given before Allah.
try: If anything you own came from bending your word, find one way to make it right this week.

title: What you have runs out. What Allah has remains.
subtitle: The patient are rewarded by their best deeds
then: Ibn Kathir says what people have {trap}will come to an end and vanish, because it is there only for a limited time{/trap}, while {reward}Allah's reward in Paradise remains without end.{/reward} He says Allah swears to reward the patient by their best deeds, forgiving the bad.
now: Your phone battery drains, your bank balance dips by the end of the month, your favorite jacket wears thin. {trap}Everything you hold is running down.{/trap} {reward}What you send ahead to Allah never runs out.{/reward}
old: What I own now is what really counts.
new: Everything I own runs out; what I give for Allah stays.
try: Give a small sadaqah today and think of it as the part that stays.

title: Man or woman, a believer who does good gets a good life.
subtitle: A promise for this world and the next
